# Overview

Asthma is a chronic disease of the lungs that affects the airways, which are the tubes that carry air into and out of the lungs.

In asthma, the airways can become inflamed and narrowed. This can make it harder for air to move through the lungs and can cause symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness.

When asthma symptoms become worse than usual, this is called an asthma attack or flare-up.

Asthma can affect people of all ages and often begins during childhood, although it can also begin during adulthood.

# Causes

The exact cause of asthma is not known.

Genetic and environmental factors both appear to play a role in whether a person develops asthma.

Asthma symptoms can become worse when a person is exposed to substances or situations called asthma triggers.

Different people can have different triggers, and a person's triggers can change over time.

## Allergic Asthma

Allergic asthma occurs when asthma symptoms are triggered by allergens.

Common allergens include:

- Dust mites
- Mold
- Pets
- Pollen from grass, trees, and weeds
- Cockroach and mouse waste

## Nonallergic Asthma

Nonallergic asthma can be triggered by things that are not allergens.

Possible triggers include:

- Cold air
- Certain medicines
- Household chemicals
- Respiratory infections such as colds and flu
- Outdoor air pollution
- Tobacco smoke

## Occupational Asthma

Occupational asthma can occur when a person is exposed to chemicals, industrial dust, or other substances at work that trigger asthma symptoms.

## Exercise-Related Symptoms

Physical exercise can trigger asthma symptoms in some people, particularly when the air is dry.

# Common Asthma Triggers

Asthma triggers vary from person to person.

Common triggers can include:

- Allergens
- Dust
- Mold
- Pollen
- Pets
- Cockroaches
- Respiratory infections
- Cold or dry air
- Tobacco smoke
- Air pollution
- Certain chemicals
- Certain medicines
- Physical exercise

Identifying and avoiding personal triggers can be an important part of asthma management.

# Risk Factors

Factors that can increase the risk of asthma include:

- Family history of asthma
- Genetic factors
- Allergies
- Obesity
- Exposure to secondhand tobacco smoke
- Exposure to certain chemicals or industrial dusts at work
- Repeated viral respiratory infections during childhood
- Certain environmental exposures

Asthma can occur in people without an obvious family history or known risk factor.

# Symptoms

Common symptoms of asthma include:

- Wheezing
- Coughing
- Shortness of breath
- Chest tightness

Coughing may be especially noticeable at night or early in the morning.

Symptoms can range from mild to severe.

Some people experience symptoms every day, while others have symptoms only occasionally.

# Asthma Attacks

An asthma attack occurs when asthma symptoms become significantly worse.

During an attack, the airways can become more narrowed and inflamed, making breathing more difficult.

Asthma attacks can develop gradually or suddenly.

Symptoms during an attack can include:

- Severe coughing
- Increased wheezing
- Significant shortness of breath
- Difficulty breathing
- Increased chest tightness

Severe asthma attacks can be life-threatening.

People who experience repeated asthma attacks may need their treatment plan reviewed by a health care provider.

# Diagnosis

A health care provider may use several methods to diagnose asthma.

These can include:

- Medical history
- Physical examination
- Lung function tests
- Spirometry
- Peak expiratory flow testing
- Tests that measure how the airways respond to specific exposures
- Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) testing
- Allergy skin tests
- Allergy blood tests

## Spirometry

Spirometry is a lung function test that measures how well a person can move air in and out of the lungs.

It can help a health care provider evaluate airflow limitation and assess whether asthma may be present.

# Treatment and Management

Asthma treatment aims to control symptoms, prevent asthma attacks, and maintain normal lung function.

Treatment plans vary depending on the person's condition and severity.

A health care provider may recommend:

- Avoiding known asthma triggers
- Quick-relief medicines
- Long-term controller medicines
- Regular monitoring
- An individualized asthma action plan

# Quick-Relief Medicines

Quick-relief medicines are used to relieve asthma symptoms quickly, including symptoms that occur during an asthma attack.

Many quick-relief medicines work by relaxing the muscles around the airways and helping open them.

A health care provider determines which medicine is appropriate and how it should be used.

# Controller Medicines

Controller medicines are taken regularly to help prevent asthma symptoms and asthma attacks.

Some controller medicines work by reducing inflammation in the airways.

They are generally used regularly according to the treatment plan, even when symptoms are not present.

A health care provider determines which controller medicine is appropriate.

# Avoiding Triggers

Avoiding known triggers can help reduce asthma symptoms.

Examples include:

- Avoiding tobacco smoke
- Reducing exposure to known allergens
- Managing exposure to workplace chemicals or dust
- Taking precautions during periods of high air pollution
- Managing respiratory infections
- Following the asthma management plan provided by a health care professional

Trigger avoidance should be individualized because triggers differ between people.

# Asthma and Exercise

Exercise can trigger symptoms in some people with asthma.

However, physical activity can still be part of a healthy lifestyle.

People who experience exercise-related asthma symptoms should discuss appropriate prevention and treatment strategies with a health care provider.

# Long-Term Management

Asthma is a chronic condition, so ongoing management may be necessary.

Long-term management can include:

- Taking prescribed controller medicines as directed
- Knowing personal asthma triggers
- Monitoring symptoms
- Using prescribed quick-relief medicines appropriately
- Following an asthma action plan
- Having regular medical follow-up

Treatment may need to be adjusted when symptoms are not adequately controlled.

# When Emergency Care May Be Needed

A severe asthma attack can become life-threatening.

Emergency medical care may be needed when severe breathing difficulty occurs or when prescribed quick-relief treatment does not adequately improve the symptoms.

A person experiencing severe difficulty breathing should seek urgent medical attention rather than relying only on information from this document.

# Important Safety Note

This document provides general medical information for educational purposes.

It does not diagnose asthma, determine whether a person has asthma, or provide a personalized treatment plan.

Asthma medicines, inhaler use, and treatment changes should be discussed with a qualified health care professional.

# Source

MedlinePlus — Asthma

# Overview

The common cold is a mild infection of the upper respiratory tract, which includes the nose and throat.

Colds are among the most common illnesses. Adults have an average of two to three colds each year, while children may have more.

Colds can occur at any time of year, although they are often more common during colder seasons.

# Causes

More than 200 different viruses can cause the common cold.

Rhinoviruses are the most common viruses associated with colds.

Because colds are caused by viruses, antibiotics do not treat the common cold.

# How Colds Spread

Cold viruses are highly contagious.

They can spread through:

- Airborne respiratory droplets
- Close personal contact
- Touching contaminated surfaces
- Touching the eyes, nose, or mouth after contact with a virus

A person can become infected after contact with respiratory secretions from someone who has a cold or after touching a contaminated object and then touching their face.

People are often most contagious during the first few days of a cold.

# Symptoms

Common symptoms include:

- Runny nose
- Stuffy or congested nose
- Sneezing
- Sore throat
- Cough
- Headache

Other symptoms can include:

- Fatigue
- Mild fever
- Chills
- Muscle aches
- Decreased appetite
- Postnasal drip

Symptoms often begin a few days after exposure to the virus.

The exact symptoms can vary depending on the virus causing the infection.

# Common Cold and Fever

Adults and older children with a cold often have a low fever or no fever.

Young children may be more likely to develop a fever.

A high or persistent fever may suggest another infection or illness and may require medical evaluation.

# Duration

Most people recover from a common cold within about one to two weeks.

Some symptoms, particularly cough or nasal symptoms, can last longer.

Symptoms that persist without improvement or that become worse after initially improving may require medical evaluation.

# Diagnosis

A common cold is usually diagnosed based on symptoms and medical history.

Most people do not need laboratory testing.

Because symptoms of a cold can overlap with illnesses such as influenza, COVID-19, and allergies, additional evaluation or testing may sometimes be appropriate.

# Treatment

There is no cure that eliminates the common cold.

Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms while the body recovers from the viral infection.

Helpful measures can include:

- Getting adequate rest
- Drinking plenty of fluids
- Using a clean humidifier or cool-mist vaporizer
- Gargling with warm salt water
- Using saline nasal drops or sprays

Over-the-counter medicines may help relieve certain symptoms.

These medicines do not cure the underlying viral infection.

# Over-the-Counter Medicines

Some over-the-counter medicines can help relieve symptoms such as pain, fever, congestion, cough, or sore throat.

People should read medicine labels carefully and follow the instructions.

Some combination cold and cough products contain more than one active ingredient. Taking additional medicines containing the same ingredient can result in taking too much of that medicine.

People taking prescription medicines or managing chronic medical conditions should ask a health care provider or pharmacist which over-the-counter medicines are appropriate.

# Antibiotics

Antibiotics do not treat the common cold.

The common cold is caused by viruses, while antibiotics are medicines used to treat certain bacterial infections.

Taking antibiotics when they are not needed can cause side effects and contributes to antibiotic resistance.

A change in the color of nasal mucus does not by itself mean that antibiotics are needed.

# Children and Cold Medicines

Some cold and cough medicines are not appropriate for young children.

Children and teenagers should not be given aspirin because of the risk of serious complications.

Parents and caregivers should ask a child's health care provider or pharmacist about appropriate medicines and doses.

Medicine labels should always be checked carefully.

# Rest and Fluids

Rest and adequate fluid intake can help support recovery and prevent dehydration.

Warm liquids and salt-water gargles may help relieve some throat symptoms.

A humidifier may help reduce discomfort from dry air, but the device should be kept clean.

# Prevention

There is no vaccine that prevents all common colds because many different viruses can cause them.

Measures that can reduce the risk of getting or spreading a cold include:

- Washing hands frequently with soap and water
- Using alcohol-based hand sanitizer when appropriate
- Avoiding touching the eyes, nose, and mouth with unwashed hands
- Avoiding close contact with people who are sick
- Avoiding sharing cups and eating utensils when someone is sick
- Cleaning frequently touched surfaces
- Covering coughs and sneezes
- Throwing used tissues away
- Staying home when sick

# Common Cold and Asthma

Respiratory infections such as the common cold can trigger wheezing and worsen asthma symptoms in some people with asthma.

People with asthma should follow the asthma management plan provided by their health care professional.

Difficulty breathing during a respiratory infection requires medical attention.

# Possible Complications

Most colds resolve without serious problems.

However, complications can occur.

Possible complications include:

- Bronchitis
- Ear infection
- Sinusitis
- Pneumonia
- Worsening of asthma symptoms

Complications are more likely in certain people, including those with weakened immune systems or underlying respiratory conditions.

# Common Cold vs Flu

The common cold and influenza can have overlapping symptoms.

Cold symptoms commonly include:

- Runny nose
- Nasal congestion
- Sneezing
- Sore throat
- Cough
- Headache

Influenza is caused by influenza viruses and can more commonly cause fever, muscle aches, fatigue, and more sudden illness.

Symptoms alone may not always reliably distinguish a cold from influenza or COVID-19.

Medical testing may be appropriate in some situations.

# When to Seek Medical Care

Medical evaluation may be needed when:

- There is difficulty breathing
- Breathing becomes unusually fast
- Signs of dehydration occur
- Fever lasts longer than four days
- Symptoms last more than ten days without improvement
- Symptoms improve and then return or become worse
- A chronic medical condition becomes worse

Severe symptoms should receive prompt medical evaluation.

# Important Safety Note

This document provides general medical information for educational purposes.

It does not diagnose a common cold or determine whether symptoms are caused by a cold, influenza, COVID-19, allergies, or another condition.

Children, older adults, pregnant people, and people with chronic medical conditions may require different medical guidance.

Medicine selection and dosing should be discussed with an appropriate health care professional when needed.

# Overview

Diabetes, also called diabetes mellitus, is a chronic disease in which blood glucose, or blood sugar, levels become too high.

Glucose is an important source of energy for the body. It comes from the food a person eats and is also produced by the body.

Insulin is a hormone made by the pancreas. It helps glucose move from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy.

In diabetes, the body may not make enough insulin, may not use insulin effectively, or both. As a result, too much glucose remains in the blood.

Persistently high blood glucose can eventually contribute to serious health problems, but appropriate management can help reduce the risk of complications.

## Type 1 Diabetes

In type 1 diabetes, the body's immune system attacks and destroys the cells in the pancreas that produce insulin.

As a result, the body makes little or no insulin.

Type 1 diabetes can occur at any age but often begins during childhood, adolescence, or young adulthood.

People with type 1 diabetes need insulin every day.

## Type 2 Diabetes

Type 2 diabetes is the most common form of diabetes.

In type 2 diabetes, the body's cells do not respond normally to insulin. This is called insulin resistance.

The pancreas may initially produce more insulin to compensate, but over time it may not be able to produce enough insulin to keep blood glucose within a healthy range.

Type 2 diabetes usually develops gradually, and some people may have few or no noticeable symptoms for a long time.

## Gestational Diabetes

Gestational diabetes is diabetes that develops during pregnancy in a person who did not already have diabetes.

It occurs when the body cannot make enough additional insulin to meet the increased needs of pregnancy.

Gestational diabetes often does not cause noticeable symptoms and is usually detected through screening during pregnancy.

People who have had gestational diabetes have an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes later.

# Causes

Different types of diabetes have different causes.

Type 1 diabetes is associated with an immune system reaction that destroys insulin-producing cells. Genetic and environmental factors may contribute.

Type 2 diabetes results from several factors, including insulin resistance, genetics, and lifestyle-related factors.

Gestational diabetes is associated with hormonal changes during pregnancy together with genetic and lifestyle factors.

# Risk Factors

Risk factors vary depending on the type of diabetes.

Risk factors for type 2 diabetes can include:

- Overweight or obesity
- Physical inactivity
- Family history of diabetes
- Increasing age
- Prediabetes
- Previous gestational diabetes
- Certain medical conditions, including high blood pressure
- Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
- Certain patterns of blood lipid levels

Not everyone with type 2 diabetes is overweight or obese.

Risk factors for gestational diabetes can include:

- Overweight or obesity
- Family history of diabetes
- Previous gestational diabetes
- Previous delivery of a large baby
- Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)

# Symptoms

Possible symptoms of diabetes include:

- Increased thirst
- Increased hunger
- Frequent urination, including urination at night
- Fatigue
- Blurred vision
- Numbness or tingling in the hands or feet
- Sores that do not heal
- Unexplained weight loss

Symptoms can vary depending on the type of diabetes.

Symptoms of type 1 diabetes often develop relatively quickly and can become severe.

Type 2 diabetes often develops gradually. Some people may have mild symptoms or no noticeable symptoms for a long period.

Gestational diabetes often causes no symptoms.

# Diabetes and Blood Glucose

Blood glucose, or blood sugar, is the main sugar found in the blood and is an important source of energy.

After food is digested, glucose enters the bloodstream.

Insulin helps glucose move from the bloodstream into cells.

When the body cannot produce enough insulin or cannot use insulin effectively, glucose can build up in the blood.

Persistently high blood glucose can damage blood vessels and organs over time.

# Diagnosis

Health care providers use blood glucose tests to diagnose diabetes.

Common tests include:

## A1C Test

The A1C test measures average blood glucose levels over approximately the previous three months.

An A1C result of 6.5 percent or higher is in the diabetes range.

An A1C result between 5.7 and 6.4 percent is in the prediabetes range.

An A1C result below 5.7 percent is generally considered within the normal range.

## Fasting Blood Glucose Test

A fasting blood glucose test measures blood glucose after a period without eating.

A fasting blood glucose level of 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or higher is in the diabetes range.

## Oral Glucose Tolerance Test

During an oral glucose tolerance test, blood glucose is measured after a person drinks a glucose-containing liquid.

A blood glucose level of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher two hours after the glucose drink is in the diabetes range.

## Random Blood Glucose Test

A random blood glucose test measures blood glucose at a particular time without requiring fasting.

When a person has symptoms of diabetes, a random blood glucose level of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher may indicate diabetes.

A health care provider determines which tests are appropriate and whether testing should be repeated.

# Treatment and Management

Treatment depends on the type of diabetes and the individual's health situation.

## Type 1 Diabetes

People with type 1 diabetes need insulin because their bodies produce little or no insulin.

Insulin can be administered by injection or through an insulin pump.

Blood glucose monitoring is also an important part of diabetes management.

## Type 2 Diabetes

Type 2 diabetes management may include:

- Healthy eating
- Regular physical activity
- Maintaining or reaching a healthy weight when appropriate
- Monitoring blood glucose
- Diabetes medicines when needed
- Regular medical follow-up

Some people with type 2 diabetes can improve their blood glucose levels substantially through lifestyle changes, while others require medicines.

Medicines can include oral medicines, insulin, and other injectable medicines.

## Gestational Diabetes

Management of gestational diabetes may include healthy eating, physical activity appropriate for pregnancy, blood glucose monitoring, and medicines when needed.

Treatment decisions during pregnancy should be made with a qualified health care provider.

# Blood Glucose Monitoring

Monitoring blood glucose can be an important part of diabetes management.

The appropriate frequency of monitoring depends on the person's type of diabetes, treatment, and medical situation.

Some people use blood glucose meters, while others may use continuous glucose monitoring systems.

A health care provider can recommend an appropriate monitoring approach.

# Low Blood Sugar

Low blood glucose is called hypoglycemia.

For many people with diabetes, a blood glucose reading below 70 mg/dL is considered low, although individual targets may differ.

Possible symptoms include:

- Shaking
- Sweating
- Hunger
- Dizziness
- Nervousness or anxiety
- Irritability
- Confusion

Low blood glucose can become dangerous if it is severe.

People with diabetes should learn from their health care provider how to recognize and manage low blood glucose.

# High Blood Sugar

High blood glucose is called hyperglycemia.

It can occur when the body does not have enough effective insulin or when diabetes is not adequately controlled.

Symptoms of high blood glucose can include increased thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, and blurred vision.

Persistent high blood glucose can contribute to long-term diabetes complications.

# Complications

Over time, diabetes can contribute to several serious health problems.

Possible complications include:

- Eye disease and vision loss
- Kidney disease
- Nerve damage
- Foot problems and infections
- Heart disease
- Heart attack
- Stroke
- Problems with blood circulation
- Increased susceptibility to certain infections

High blood glucose can damage blood vessels and nerves.

Diabetes-related nerve damage may reduce the ability to feel pain, pressure, heat, or cold in the feet. This can make injuries more difficult to notice.

Good management of blood glucose, blood pressure, and cholesterol can help reduce the risk of complications.

# Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes

Type 1 diabetes cannot currently be prevented.

Some cases of type 2 diabetes can be prevented or delayed through lifestyle changes.

Helpful measures can include:

- Regular physical activity
- Healthy eating
- Maintaining a healthy weight
- Losing weight when appropriate for people who are overweight
- Managing other health conditions that increase diabetes risk

People with risk factors for diabetes should discuss screening and prevention with a health care provider.

# Diabetes and Long-Term Monitoring

Diabetes management involves more than monitoring blood glucose.

Regular medical care may include monitoring:

- Blood glucose
- A1C
- Blood pressure
- Cholesterol
- Kidney health
- Eye health
- Foot health

The exact monitoring schedule depends on the individual's type of diabetes and health situation.

# When Medical Attention May Be Needed

A person with diabetes should seek medical advice when symptoms are new, worsening, difficult to control, or when blood glucose repeatedly falls outside the range recommended by their health care provider.

Severe symptoms associated with very low blood glucose can be an emergency.

Severe illness, confusion, loss of consciousness, seizures, or other serious symptoms require urgent medical evaluation.

# Important Safety Note

This document provides general medical information for educational purposes.

It does not diagnose diabetes, determine whether a person has diabetes, or provide a personalized treatment plan.

Blood glucose values and treatment decisions should be interpreted in the context of the individual's health history and by a qualified health care professional.

# Source

MedlinePlus — Diabetes

https://medlineplus.gov/diabetes.html

# Fever

Fever is a body temperature that is higher than normal. A normal body temperature varies from person to person, but it is generally around 98.6°F (37°C). A temperature above 100.4°F (38°C) most often means that a person has a fever.

## What causes fever?

Fever is usually a sign that the body is responding to an illness or infection. Infections are a common cause of fever. Fever can occur with many different illnesses and does not itself identify a specific disease.

## Symptoms associated with fever

Fever may occur along with other symptoms depending on its cause. Common symptoms that can occur with fever include chills, feeling cold, sweating, headache, muscle aches, fatigue, and decreased appetite.

## Fever and medical evaluation

The significance of a fever depends on factors such as the person's age, temperature, duration of the fever, and other symptoms. A persistent or high fever, or a fever accompanied by concerning symptoms, may require medical evaluation.

## General information

Fever is part of the body's response to illness or infection. It is a symptom rather than a disease itself. The underlying cause of a fever determines what other symptoms may occur and whether medical evaluation is needed.

# Overview

Gastroesophageal reflux disease, commonly called GERD, is a chronic condition in which stomach contents move backward from the stomach into the esophagus.

The esophagus is the tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach.

Occasional acid reflux is common. GERD occurs when reflux happens frequently or causes symptoms or damage to the esophagus.

GERD can affect adults, children, and infants.

# How GERD Happens

A ring of muscle at the lower end of the esophagus helps prevent stomach contents from moving backward.

This muscle is called the lower esophageal sphincter (LES).

If the LES becomes weak or relaxes at the wrong time, stomach contents can move back into the esophagus.

Stomach acid and other stomach contents can irritate the lining of the esophagus and cause symptoms.

# Causes and Risk Factors

GERD can occur when the lower esophageal sphincter does not close properly.

Factors that can increase the likelihood of GERD include:

- Overweight or obesity
- Pregnancy
- Hiatal hernia
- Smoking
- Exposure to secondhand smoke
- Lying down soon after eating

Certain foods, drinks, and medicines can also make reflux symptoms worse.

# Common Symptoms

The most common symptom of GERD is heartburn.

Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest or throat that occurs when stomach contents move upward into the esophagus.

Other possible symptoms include:

- Acid or food coming back into the mouth
- Regurgitation
- Dry cough
- Hoarse voice
- Asthma-like symptoms
- Trouble swallowing
- Sore throat
- Nausea
- Hiccups

A person can have GERD without experiencing heartburn.

Symptoms may become worse after eating, when bending over, or when lying down.

Symptoms can also be worse at night.

# Heartburn and GERD

Heartburn is a common symptom of acid reflux.

Occasional heartburn does not necessarily mean that a person has GERD.

Frequent heartburn, especially when it occurs repeatedly or causes other problems, may be associated with GERD.

GERD can also occur without typical heartburn.

# Diagnosis

A health care provider may diagnose GERD based on symptoms and medical history.

Some people with mild symptoms may not need diagnostic tests.

When additional evaluation is needed, tests can include:

- Upper GI endoscopy
- Esophageal pH testing
- Esophageal manometry
- Esophageal impedance testing
- Upper gastrointestinal imaging in selected situations

# Upper GI Endoscopy

An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy allows a health care provider to examine the lining of the esophagus and stomach using a flexible tube with a small camera.

A biopsy may be performed during an endoscopy when tissue needs to be examined.

Endoscopy may be recommended when symptoms are severe, persistent, or return after treatment, or when complications are suspected.

# Esophageal pH Testing

Esophageal pH testing measures how often stomach acid enters the esophagus and how long acid remains there.

This testing can help evaluate whether symptoms are associated with acid reflux.

# Esophageal Manometry

Esophageal manometry measures pressure and movement in the esophagus.

It can help evaluate how well the esophagus and lower esophageal sphincter function.

# Treatment

Most people can manage GERD with lifestyle changes and medicines.

Treatment depends on the person's symptoms and medical situation.

Treatment options may include:

- Lifestyle changes
- Over-the-counter medicines
- Prescription medicines
- In some cases, procedures or surgery

# Lifestyle Management

Lifestyle measures that may help reduce GERD symptoms include:

- Eating smaller meals
- Avoiding lying down for at least 2 to 3 hours after eating
- Avoiding foods that trigger symptoms
- Losing weight when appropriate
- Raising the head of the bed when symptoms occur at night
- Quitting smoking
- Avoiding alcohol when it worsens symptoms

Common foods or drinks that may trigger symptoms in some people include:

- Spicy foods
- Fatty foods
- Chocolate
- Caffeine

Triggers vary between individuals.

# Medicines

Several types of medicines can be used to manage GERD.

## Antacids

Antacids neutralize stomach acid and can provide short-term relief from heartburn.

They do not treat all causes or complications of GERD.

## H2 Blockers

H2 blockers reduce the amount of acid produced by the stomach.

They may provide longer-lasting relief than antacids.

## Proton Pump Inhibitors

Proton pump inhibitors, or PPIs, reduce stomach acid production.

They are commonly used to treat GERD and acid-related damage to the esophagus.

Medication choice and duration should be determined with appropriate medical guidance.

## Potassium-Competitive Acid Blockers

Potassium-competitive acid blockers, or P-CABs, are another class of medicines that reduce stomach acid.

A health care provider can determine whether a particular medicine is appropriate.

# GERD and Medications

Some medicines can worsen heartburn or reflux symptoms.

Examples can include certain medicines used for:

- High blood pressure
- Heart disease
- Asthma
- Parkinson disease
- Anxiety or insomnia

A person should not stop or change a prescribed medicine without discussing it with a health care professional.

# Complications

Untreated or persistent GERD can sometimes cause complications.

Possible complications include:

- Inflammation of the esophagus
- Esophageal ulcers
- Scarring and narrowing of the esophagus
- Barrett's esophagus
- Chronic cough
- Chronic hoarseness
- Worsening of asthma symptoms
- Dental problems

Barrett's esophagus involves changes in the lining of the esophagus and can increase the risk of esophageal cancer.

# GERD and Asthma

GERD can be associated with asthma-like symptoms and may worsen asthma in some people.

Persistent cough or breathing-related symptoms should not automatically be assumed to be caused by GERD because other conditions can cause similar symptoms.

# Prevention and Symptom Reduction

Measures that may help reduce GERD symptoms include:

- Maintaining a healthy body weight
- Eating smaller meals
- Avoiding personal trigger foods
- Avoiding meals close to bedtime
- Remaining upright after eating
- Avoiding tobacco
- Limiting alcohol when it worsens symptoms
- Raising the head of the bed when nighttime symptoms occur

Not every measure works equally well for every person.

# When to Contact a Health Care Provider

Medical evaluation may be appropriate when:

- GERD symptoms occur frequently
- Symptoms do not improve with lifestyle changes
- Symptoms continue despite treatment
- Food feels stuck when swallowing
- Swallowing is painful or difficult
- There is unexplained weight loss
- There is frequent vomiting
- There is loss of appetite
- There is bleeding
- Persistent cough or hoarseness occurs

# Emergency Warning Signs

Chest pain can have causes other than GERD.

Chest pain accompanied by shortness of breath or pain in the jaw or arm can be a sign of a heart problem and requires urgent medical attention.

Vomiting blood or passing black, tarry stools can also require urgent medical evaluation.

# Important Safety Note

This document provides general medical information for educational purposes.

It does not diagnose GERD or determine the cause of a person's symptoms.

Chest pain should not automatically be assumed to be heartburn or GERD.

Medication changes and treatment decisions should be made with a qualified health care professional.

https://medlineplus.gov/gerd.html

## Overview

High blood pressure, also called hypertension, occurs when the force of blood pushing against the walls of the arteries is too high.

A blood pressure reading has two numbers:

- Systolic pressure: the pressure when the heart beats.
- Diastolic pressure: the pressure when the heart is resting between beats.

For example, a blood pressure reading of 120/80 means a systolic pressure of 120 and a diastolic pressure of 80.

## Symptoms

High blood pressure usually has no symptoms. Regular blood pressure measurements are therefore important for detecting it.

Very high blood pressure can be dangerous and may require immediate medical attention.

## Blood Pressure Categories

For adults, MedlinePlus lists the following categories:

- Normal: systolic below 120 and diastolic below 80.
- Elevated: systolic 120–129 and diastolic below 80.
- Stage 1 high blood pressure: systolic 130–139 or diastolic 80–89.
- Stage 2 high blood pressure: systolic 140 or higher or diastolic 90 or higher.
- Hypertensive crisis: systolic higher than 180 and diastolic higher than 120. Seek medical care right away.

A healthcare provider considers multiple blood pressure measurements when diagnosing hypertension.

## Types

There are two main types of high blood pressure:

### Primary hypertension

Primary, or essential, hypertension is the most common type. It generally develops over time, often as people get older.

### Secondary hypertension

Secondary hypertension is caused by another medical condition or by certain medicines. Treating the underlying condition or stopping the causative medicine may improve the blood pressure.

## Risk Factors and Causes

Factors associated with high blood pressure can include:

- Older age
- Family history
- Obesity
- High sodium intake
- Physical inactivity
- Diabetes
- Tobacco use
- Excessive alcohol consumption
- Certain medical conditions
- Certain medicines

In many people with primary hypertension, no single specific cause can be identified.

## Health Risks

Persistently high blood pressure can increase the risk of serious health problems, including:

- Heart attack
- Stroke
- Heart failure
- Kidney disease
- Eye problems

## Diagnosis

High blood pressure is diagnosed using blood pressure measurements.

A healthcare provider may take multiple readings at different appointments before making a diagnosis.

Blood pressure can vary depending on factors such as the time of day and other circumstances, so a single measurement does not necessarily establish a diagnosis.

## Treatment

Treatment can include:

- Heart-healthy lifestyle changes
- Physical activity
- Healthy eating
- Reducing sodium intake
- Maintaining a healthy weight
- Managing stress
- Medicines when appropriate

The appropriate treatment plan depends on the person's blood pressure and other health factors. Treatment decisions should be made with a healthcare provider.

## Important Safety Note

This document provides general educational information. It is not a diagnosis or individualized medical advice. A healthcare professional should be consulted for diagnosis and treatment decisions.

# Overview

A migraine is a recurring type of headache that can cause moderate to severe pain. The pain is often throbbing or pulsing and is frequently felt on one side of the head.

Migraine is a neurological condition that can cause symptoms in addition to headache. These may include nausea, vomiting, sensitivity to light and sound, dizziness, weakness, and changes in vision.

Some people experience migraine attacks with an aura, while others have migraine without aura.

# Causes

The exact sequence of events that causes a migraine is not completely understood.

Genetic factors appear to play an important role. Many people with migraine have family members who also experience migraines.

Migraine attacks can be triggered by different factors, and triggers vary from person to person.

# Common Migraine Triggers

Possible triggers include:

- Stress
- Anxiety
- Hormonal changes
- Changes in sleep patterns
- Too little or too much sleep
- Skipping meals
- Dehydration
- Bright or flashing lights
- Loud noises
- Strong smells
- Sudden weather or environmental changes
- Physical overexertion
- Tobacco smoke
- Caffeine
- Caffeine withdrawal
- Alcohol
- Certain medicines
- Medication overuse

Some people also report certain foods as triggers, including chocolate, aged cheeses, processed meats, fermented or pickled foods, and foods containing MSG.

Triggers are highly individual. A food or activity that triggers a migraine in one person may not trigger one in another person.

# Risk Factors

Migraine can affect people of all ages.

Factors associated with a higher likelihood of migraine include:

- Family history of migraine
- Being female
- Hormonal changes
- Certain sleep disorders
- Depression or anxiety
- Bipolar disorder
- Epilepsy

Migraine can occur in children as well as adults.

# Types of Migraine

Two common forms are:

- Migraine with aura
- Migraine without aura

Migraine without aura is common and occurs without the neurological warning symptoms known as aura.

# Migraine Phases

A migraine attack can occur in several phases.

A person does not necessarily experience every phase during every migraine attack.

## Prodrome

The prodrome phase can occur before the headache.

Possible symptoms include:

- Food cravings
- Mood changes
- Yawning
- Fatigue
- Increased urination
- Fluid retention

Prodrome symptoms can begin hours before the headache.

## Aura

Aura consists of temporary neurological symptoms that can occur before or during a migraine.

Visual symptoms can include:

- Flashing lights
- Zigzag lines
- Bright spots
- Blind spots
- Changes in vision

Other aura symptoms can include:

- Numbness
- Tingling
- Weakness
- Difficulty finding words
- Changes in sensation

Not everyone with migraine experiences aura.

## Headache Phase

The headache phase often begins gradually and can become more severe.

The pain is commonly:

- Throbbing
- Pulsing
- Moderate to severe
- More noticeable on one side of the head

Other symptoms may include:

- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Sensitivity to light
- Sensitivity to sound
- Sensitivity to odors
- Pain that becomes worse with movement

Some people can experience migraine symptoms without having a typical headache.

## Postdrome

After the headache ends, some people experience a postdrome phase.

Possible symptoms include:

- Fatigue
- Weakness
- Difficulty concentrating
- Feeling mentally unclear
- Neck discomfort

# Duration

Migraine headaches can last from several hours to several days.

A typical untreated migraine attack can last approximately 4 to 72 hours.

The exact duration varies between individuals and attacks.

# Diagnosis

There is no single laboratory test that proves a person has migraine.

A health care provider may diagnose migraine by evaluating:

- Symptoms
- Headache pattern
- Medical history
- Family history
- Physical examination
- Neurological examination

The provider may also evaluate other possible causes of headache.

# Diagnostic Tests

Most people with typical migraine symptoms do not require special imaging tests.

Additional tests may be considered when symptoms are unusual or when another medical condition needs to be ruled out.

Possible tests include:

- CT scan
- MRI
- Blood tests
- Electroencephalogram (EEG) in selected situations
- Lumbar puncture in selected situations

The need for testing depends on the person's symptoms and medical history.

# Treatment

There is currently no cure for migraine, but treatment can help relieve symptoms and reduce the frequency or severity of attacks.

Treatment can include:

- Medicines to treat an acute migraine attack
- Medicines to prevent migraine attacks
- Lifestyle changes
- Trigger management
- Rest and hydration

Treatment should be selected with consideration of the person's medical history and other medicines.

# Treating a Migraine Attack

During a migraine attack, some people may benefit from:

- Resting in a quiet, dark room
- Closing the eyes
- Drinking fluids
- Using a cool cloth or ice pack on the forehead

For some people, medicines may also be used.

Over-the-counter pain medicines can sometimes help with mild migraine symptoms.

Prescription medicines may be used when over-the-counter medicines are not effective or when migraines are more severe.

Some prescription migraine medicines include triptans and medicines that target calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP).

A health care provider can determine which treatment is appropriate.

# Preventive Treatment

Preventive treatment may be considered when migraine attacks are frequent or significantly interfere with daily life.

Preventive medicines may include certain:

- Blood pressure medicines
- Antidepressants
- Anti-seizure medicines
- CGRP-targeting medicines

Botulinum toxin type A may be used for selected people with chronic migraine.

Treatment decisions should be made with a health care professional.

# Lifestyle Management

Lifestyle measures can help some people reduce migraine frequency or severity.

Helpful strategies may include:

- Maintaining a regular sleep schedule
- Eating regular meals
- Staying adequately hydrated
- Managing stress
- Exercising regularly when appropriate
- Avoiding known personal triggers
- Avoiding tobacco
- Limiting or avoiding alcohol when it triggers migraines
- Managing caffeine intake

A headache diary can help identify patterns and possible triggers.

# Headache Diary

A headache diary can record:

- Date and time the headache started
- What was eaten and drank
- Amount and quality of sleep
- Activities before the headache
- Possible triggers
- Symptoms experienced
- Medicines taken
- How long the headache lasted
- What helped relieve the symptoms

Sharing this information with a health care provider can help with diagnosis and treatment planning.

# Medication Overuse

Using headache medicines too frequently can cause medication-overuse headaches, sometimes called rebound headaches.

Repeated use of pain medicines can cause headaches to become more frequent or difficult to control.

People who regularly need headache medicine several days per week should discuss this with a health care provider.

# Migraine and Hormones

Hormonal changes can trigger migraine attacks in some people.

Some people experience migraines around menstruation.

Hormonal changes during pregnancy or with hormonal medicines can also affect migraine patterns.

Hormonal factors vary significantly between individuals.

# When to Seek Medical Attention

A headache should receive urgent medical evaluation when it:

- Starts suddenly and is extremely severe
- Is described as the worst headache of a person's life
- Occurs with new problems speaking
- Occurs with new vision problems
- Occurs with weakness or loss of movement
- Occurs with loss of balance
- Occurs with confusion or loss of alertness
- Occurs with fever
- Is substantially different from previous headaches

These symptoms can sometimes indicate a condition other than migraine.

# Important Safety Note

This document provides general medical information for educational purposes.

It does not diagnose migraine or determine the cause of a person's headache.

A new, sudden, unusually severe, or significantly different headache should not automatically be assumed to be a migraine.

Medication selection, dosage, and preventive treatment should be discussed with a qualified health care professional.

# Overview

Pneumonia is an infection in one or both lungs. It causes the air sacs in the lungs to fill with fluid or pus.

Pneumonia can range from mild to severe. The severity depends on factors such as the organism causing the infection, the person's age, and overall health.

Pneumonia can affect people of any age.

# Causes

Pneumonia can be caused by different types of germs, including:

- Bacteria
- Viruses
- Fungi

Bacterial pneumonia is a common cause of pneumonia in adults.

Viral infections of the respiratory tract can also cause pneumonia. Viruses associated with pneumonia include influenza viruses, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2.

Fungal pneumonia is more common in people with weakened immune systems or certain chronic health conditions.

Pneumonia can also occur after accidentally breathing food, liquid, vomit, or other material into the lungs. This is called aspiration pneumonia.

# Types of Pneumonia

Pneumonia can be classified in several ways depending on its cause and where it was acquired.

Examples include:

- Bacterial pneumonia
- Viral pneumonia
- Fungal pneumonia
- Aspiration pneumonia
- Community-acquired pneumonia
- Hospital-acquired pneumonia

Different types may require different approaches to diagnosis and treatment.

# How Pneumonia Can Develop

Pneumonia can develop when disease-causing organisms reach the lungs.

Bacteria or viruses that are present in the nose, mouth, or upper respiratory tract can sometimes spread into the lungs.

A person can also inhale infectious particles directly.

Aspiration can occur when food, liquids, vomit, or secretions enter the lungs instead of passing normally through the digestive tract.

# Risk Factors

Anyone can develop pneumonia, but certain factors increase the risk.

Risk factors include:

- Being age 65 or older
- Being age 2 or younger
- Smoking
- Heavy alcohol use
- Malnutrition
- Chronic lung disease
- Heart disease
- Diabetes
- Liver disease
- Kidney disease
- A weakened immune system
- Difficulty coughing or swallowing
- Recent respiratory infection
- Recent surgery or trauma
- Exposure to certain chemicals, pollutants, or toxic fumes
- Recent hospitalization

People who are hospitalized, particularly those in intensive care, may have an increased risk of pneumonia.

# Symptoms

Pneumonia symptoms can range from mild to severe.

Common symptoms include:

- Cough
- Fever
- Chills
- Shortness of breath
- Chest pain when breathing or coughing
- Fatigue

Other symptoms can include:

- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Diarrhea
- Headache
- Loss of appetite
- Weakness
- Sweating

A cough may produce mucus or phlegm.

# Symptoms in Older Adults

Older adults may have different or less obvious symptoms.

They may have:

- Weakness
- Confusion
- Reduced alertness
- Lower-than-normal body temperature

Older adults and people with serious illnesses or weakened immune systems may have fewer typical symptoms even when pneumonia is serious.

# Symptoms in Infants and Children

Newborns and infants may not show typical symptoms.

Children may have:

- Fever
- Cough
- Vomiting
- Difficulty breathing
- Reduced energy
- Restlessness

Symptoms vary depending on the child's age and the cause of the infection.

# Diagnosis

Pneumonia can sometimes be difficult to distinguish from other respiratory infections because symptoms can overlap with conditions such as a cold or influenza.

A health care provider may:

- Ask about symptoms and medical history
- Perform a physical examination
- Listen to the lungs with a stethoscope
- Order imaging or laboratory tests

# Chest X-Ray

A chest X-ray is commonly used when pneumonia is suspected.

It can help show areas of infection or inflammation in the lungs.

# Blood Tests

Blood tests may be used to evaluate infection and overall health.

A complete blood count (CBC) may be performed.

Blood cultures may sometimes be used to determine whether bacteria have entered the bloodstream.

# Sputum Testing

A sputum test examines mucus produced by coughing.

It may help identify bacteria or other organisms causing pneumonia.

Sputum testing is more likely to be used when pneumonia is severe or when identifying the specific organism is important for treatment.

# Additional Tests

People who are hospitalized, have severe symptoms, are older, or have other serious health problems may need additional tests.

These may include:

- Chest CT scan
- Pulse oximetry
- Pleural fluid testing
- Bronchoscopy

Pulse oximetry measures the amount of oxygen in the blood.

# Treatment

Treatment depends on:

- The cause of the pneumonia
- The type of pneumonia
- The severity of illness
- The person's age
- Other health conditions

## Bacterial Pneumonia

Antibiotics are used to treat bacterial pneumonia.

The choice of antibiotic depends on the suspected or identified bacteria and the person's medical situation.

## Viral Pneumonia

Antibiotics do not treat viral pneumonia.

Some viral pneumonias may be treated with antiviral medicines depending on the virus and the person's circumstances.

## Fungal Pneumonia

Fungal pneumonia can require antifungal medicines.

The appropriate treatment depends on the specific fungus and the person's health condition.

# Hospital Treatment

Some people with pneumonia need treatment in a hospital.

Hospital care may be necessary when symptoms are severe or when a person has a high risk of complications.

Hospital treatment may include:

- Oxygen therapy
- Intravenous medicines
- Fluids
- Monitoring of oxygen levels
- Respiratory support

Severe cases may require mechanical ventilation.

# Recovery

Recovery time varies.

Some people begin to feel better within about a week.

For others, recovery can take a month or longer.

Older adults and people with chronic diseases or weakened immune systems may take longer to recover.

Fatigue or cough may continue for some time after the infection improves.

# Complications

Pneumonia can sometimes cause serious complications.

Possible complications include:

- Bacteremia
- Sepsis or septic shock
- Lung abscess
- Pleural disorders
- Pleural effusion
- Kidney failure
- Respiratory failure

The risk of complications is higher in certain people, including older adults, very young children, people with weakened immune systems, and people with serious chronic diseases.

# Pneumonia and Respiratory Failure

Severe pneumonia can interfere with the lungs' ability to provide enough oxygen to the body.

Respiratory failure can occur when the lungs cannot adequately exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide.

People with respiratory failure may require oxygen therapy or mechanical ventilation.

# Prevention

Some types of pneumonia can be prevented or their risk reduced.

Preventive measures include:

- Staying up to date with recommended vaccines
- Getting recommended influenza vaccination
- Asking a health care provider about pneumococcal vaccination when appropriate
- Following recommended COVID-19 vaccination guidance
- Washing hands frequently
- Avoiding tobacco smoke
- Maintaining a healthy lifestyle
- Avoiding close contact with people who are sick when possible

Vaccination recommendations depend on factors such as age and health conditions.

# Pneumonia and Smoking

Smoking damages the lungs and can make it more difficult for the respiratory system to fight infection.

Not smoking can reduce the risk of respiratory infections and other lung problems.

People who smoke can discuss smoking cessation support with a health care professional.

# Pneumonia and Chronic Conditions

Certain chronic conditions can increase the risk of severe pneumonia.

Examples include:

- Diabetes
- Heart disease
- Chronic lung disease
- Liver disease
- Kidney disease
- Conditions that weaken the immune system

People with these conditions may need additional preventive measures and medical monitoring.

# When to Seek Medical Care

Medical evaluation may be needed when a person has:

- Persistent or worsening cough
- Difficulty breathing
- Shortness of breath
- Chest pain that occurs with breathing or coughing
- Persistent fever
- Shaking chills
- Coughing up blood
- Symptoms that become worse after initially improving

People with weakened immune systems should seek medical advice promptly when symptoms of pneumonia occur.

# Emergency Warning Signs

Severe difficulty breathing can be an emergency.

Urgent medical care is needed when breathing becomes increasingly difficult, when a person becomes confused or unusually sleepy, or when severe symptoms occur.

Blue or gray discoloration of the lips or fingertips can indicate inadequate oxygen and requires urgent medical attention.

# Important Safety Note

This document provides general medical information for educational purposes.

It does not diagnose pneumonia or determine which organism is causing an infection.

Antibiotics, antivirals, antifungals, oxygen therapy, and other treatments should only be selected with appropriate medical guidance.

Difficulty breathing, severe chest symptoms, confusion, or other severe symptoms require prompt medical evaluation.
